newsitem.title: UK: UK survey sees gap between fund managers, analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK survey sees gap between fund managers, analysts.

text.p: Fund managers have markedly different ideas about how analysts should be spending their time compared with how the analysts are actually allocating their attentions.
The 1997 Reuters survey of UK larger company investment research, sales and trading found misconceptions on the part of fund managers and differences in time preferences.

While fund managers said they would like 46 percent of analysts' time to be spent on fundamental research in future, the analysts themselves said they intended spending 36.6 percent of their time on this aspect of their work.
The survey also found fund managers thought analysts spent just over 20 percent of their time on corporate finance activities but said they would prefer them to spend only seven percent on this.
Analysts said the actual time allocated to corporate finance was just over 10 percent, but said they would like to give it slightly less time.

Fund managers questioned said they thought only 11 percent of analysts' time should be devoted to selling to institutional clients, contrasting with the analysts who see this as something which should account for 26 percent of their time.

While 93 percent of fund managers highlighted fundamental company and industry research as the main priority for broking analysts' job content, nearly 91 percent of analysts said good ideas were top of their priorities, with only 81 percent citing the same factor as fund managers.
